suggestions.title: Star Wars: Episode IV - A New Hope
suggestions.description: You have been shown The Empire Strikes Back but never the film it is a sequel to - and this is the one that rebuilt the blockbuster. Lucas wrote a stripped-down hero's-journey script (farm boy, call to adventure, mentor, death star, trench run) after failing to license Flash Gordon, then spent a career's worth of energy on world-building: a used, dusty galaxy where the ships rattle and the cantina band is an actual band, starfighter dogfights cut from WWII gun-camera footage, and a final 20-minute aerial sequence that is pure silent-film editing with sound effects. Industrial Light & Magic was founded to make this film, and the practical model work still reads better than most modern CG. It won six Oscars (score, sound, editing, visual effects, art direction, costume) and made John Williams' score the most recognisable in cinema history. Watch it for the craft: Ben Burtt's sound design is the reason lightsabers have a voice, and the binary-sunset shot is a matte painting that cost less than a car. Then you can re-watch Empire with the whole thing behind it.

suggestions.title: Life Is Beautiful
suggestions.description: The highest-rated film still sitting unshown on your list that is not a war epic or a crime picture: an Italian tragicomedy that won the Grand Prix at Cannes and took three Oscars (Best Actor for Roberto Benigni, Best Foreign Language Film, Best Original Dramatic Score). It works in two halves with completely different rules. The first is a sunlit 1930s romantic comedy - Guido, a fast-talking Jewish waiter, courts Dora with a series of escalating gags, including a memorable driving-school bit, and the film is genuinely funny in the way early Chaplin is funny. The second half puts the same man and his five-year-old son inside a concentration camp, where he reframes the horror as a game with points, rules and a prize - a tank - and refuses to break character no matter what it costs him. Benigni directs with the tonal risk deliberately visible: the comedy is not relief, it is the plot. Nicola Piovani's score and the 'Buongiorno, Principessa!' payoff land hardest because of everything the film refuses to show you. Seen after Schindler's List and The Pianist on your list, this is the third, strangest and most disarming angle on the same subject.

suggestions.title: Double Indemnity
suggestions.description: Your list has 96 films on it and not one true film noir - this is where the genre is defined. Billy Wilder and Raymond Chandler (the novelist, adapting James M. Cain's novella) invented most of the moves that everything from Chinatown to Body Heat would later borrow: the confession told in flashback from a man already bleeding out, the seductive wife in an ankle bracelet, the murder staged for an insurance payout, the narration that keeps telling you it is a mistake while the character keeps walking into it. Fred MacMurray plays against his nice-guy screen image as the insurance salesman who thinks he is the smartest person in the room, Barbara Stanwyck is the coldest lead performance in 1940s Hollywood, and Edward G. Robinson's claims investigator is the quietly heartbreaking moral centre of the film. Wilder's dialogue is a machine: the seduction scene is all innuendo and speed, and the 'how fast was I going?' exchange lands like a punchline. It was nominated for seven Oscars and won none - the definitive snub-breakthrough of the era, and the third different decade in this round.
